blocks.text: The Doppler effect is also applicable to electromagnetic waves. One of its important applications is the radar system, which uses radio waves to determine the elevation and speed of an aeroplane. RADAR (RAdio Detection And Ranging) is a device which transmits and receives radio waves. If an aeroplane approaches the radar, the wavelength of the wave reflected from the aeroplane is shorter, and if it moves away the wavelength is larger (Fig. 7.13 a, b). Similarly, the speed of satellites moving around the Earth can be determined by the same principle.

blocks.alt: Two panels with a radar dish on the left and a plane on the right. The radar sends grey waves out. (a) The plane flies towards the radar and its echo comes back with waves squeezed together, a higher frequency. (b) The plane flies away and its echo has waves stretched out, a lower frequency.
blocks.caption: Radar waves reflected from an approaching (a) and a receding (b) aeroplane (original diagram after Figure 7.13).

blocks.text: SONAR is an acronym derived from Sound Navigation And Ranging. It is the general name for sonic or ultrasonic underwater echo-ranging and echo-sounding systems, a technique for detecting the presence of objects under water by acoustical echo. In sonar, Doppler detection relies upon the relative speed of the target and the detector to provide an indication of the target's speed, employing the Doppler effect, in which an apparent change in frequency occurs when the source and the observer are in relative motion. Its known military applications include the detection and location of submarines, the control of antisubmarine weapons, mine hunting, and measurement of the depth of the sea.

Astronomers use the Doppler effect to calculate the speeds of distant stars and galaxies: by comparing the line spectrum of light from the star with light from a laboratory source, the Doppler shift of the star's light can be measured and then the speed of the star calculated.

items: Stars moving away from the Earth show a red shift (Fig. 7.14b): the emitted waves have a longer wavelength than if the star were at rest, so the spectrum is shifted towards longer wavelength, the red end of the spectrum. Astronomers have discovered that all the distant galaxies are moving away from us, and by measuring their red shifts have estimated their speeds.

Stars moving towards the Earth show a blue shift (Fig. 7.14c), because the wavelength of the light emitted by the star is shorter than if the star were at rest, so the spectrum is shifted towards shorter wavelength, the blue end of the spectrum.

blocks.alt: Three spectra from violet on the left to red on the right, each with a dark line. For a star at rest the line is in its normal place; for a star moving away it is shifted towards the red end (red shift); for a star moving closer it is shifted towards the blue end (blue shift).
blocks.caption: A spectral line for a star at rest, receding (red shift) and approaching (blue shift) (original diagram after Figure 7.14).

items: Radar speed trap: microwaves are emitted from a transmitter in short bursts; each burst is reflected off any car in the path of the microwaves between bursts, and the transmitter is open to detect the reflected microwaves. If the reflection is caused by a moving obstacle, the reflected microwaves are Doppler shifted, and by measuring the Doppler shift the speed of the car is calculated by a computer programme.

Satellite navigation uses the Doppler shift to determine satellite velocity and position, enabling accurate location tracking; satellite communication uses Doppler-shift compensation to ensure stable communication signals.
Doppler radar detects wind velocity and precipitation patterns; the Doppler shift also helps to measure the Earth's surface velocity and deformation.

Doppler echocardiography measures blood-flow velocity and detects cardiac abnormalities such as valve stenosis or regurgitation, and helps optimise pacemaker settings; Doppler ultrasound measures blood flow, calculates cardiac output, and detects vascular stenosis or occlusion.

blocks.title: Example 7.12
blocks.text: The wavelength of one of the lines of the absorption spectrum of a faint galaxy, identified as the Ca-alpha line, is found to be 478 nm; the wavelength of the same line measured in the laboratory is 397 nm. (a) Is the galaxy moving towards or away from the Earth? (b) Compute the speed of the galaxy relative to the Earth. Solution: lambda = 397 nm = 397 x 10^-9 m (laboratory), lambda' = 478 nm = 478 x 10^-9 m (apparent), c = 3 x 10^8 m s^-1. (a) As v = f lambda and v = c, f = c/lambda = 3 x 10^8 / 397 x 10^-9 = 7.56 x 10^14 Hz (laboratory frequency); apparent frequency f' = c/lambda' = 3 x 10^8 / 478 x 10^-9 = 6.28 x 10^14 Hz. Since lambda' is greater than lambda, or f' is less than f, the galaxy is moving away from the Earth. (b) f' = (v/(v + u_s)) f = (c/(c + u_s)) f; putting the values, 6.28 x 10^14 = (3 x 10^8/(3 x 10^8 + u_s)) x 7.56 x 10^14, so 3 x 10^8 + u_s = 3 x 10^8 x 7.56 x 10^14 / 6.28 x 10^14, u_s = 22.68 x 10^8/6.28 - 3 x 10^8 = 6.12 x 10^7 m s^-1.

blocks.prompt: How would you apply the Doppler effect to study cardiac problems in humans (short question 7.6)? A galaxy recedes at 0.2 c; a spectral line normally emitted at 500 nm is observed at what wavelength, using the book's formula (Galactic Motion box)?
blocks.explanation: Ultrasound is beamed into the heart and blood vessels; it is reflected by moving red blood cells and returns Doppler shifted, the shift giving the speed and direction of blood flow, so narrowed (stenosed) or leaking (regurgitant) valves, blocked vessels and cardiac output can be measured. With f' = (c/(c + u_s)) f and lambda = c/f, lambda' = lambda (c + u_s)/c = 500 x 1.2 = 600 nm, a red shift of 100 nm.

items: Doppler shift of electromagnetic and sound waves: radar (aircraft and satellites), sonar (submarines, mines, sea depth), astronomy (red shift receding, blue shift approaching; all distant galaxies recede), radar speed traps, satellite navigation and communication, weather radar, echocardiography and Doppler ultrasound.
Example 7.12: 478 nm against 397 nm, f' less than f, the galaxy recedes at 6.12 x 10^7 m s^-1.
